source.title: On the Alignment Between Supervised and Self-Supervised Contrastive Learning
source.authors: Achleshwar Luthra; Priyadarsi Mishra; Tomer Galanti

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present; no apparent truncation or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: Tests representation alignment between contrastive learning and supervised objectives, and its dependence on training conditions. The results refine the scope of broad convergence claims: alignment varies with the objective and training setup, and can decline over training.
record.gate_note: The paper measures CL–NSCL alignment with CKA and RSA, compares CL against SCL and cross-entropy, and studies class count, temperature, batch size and learning-rate scaling. Downstream accuracies are not alignment results. The paper cites prior results about loss-level similarity, but those cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures CKA/RSA alignment between ResNet-50 models trained on the same data with different objectives (CL vs NSCL, SCL, CE). Alignment is high only when the objectives nearly coincide and near zero for CL–SCL. This bears narrowly on V7's claim that shared objectives, not a common model of reality, drive alignment. It is a new setting (SSL vs supervised, same architecture and data), not the originals' method. No scale sweep, cross-modal pairing, seed comparison, mapping or feature-level test is run. Training hyperparameters (temperature, class count, batch size) are not measurement choices, so V6 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that CL and NSCL representations stay closely aligned during coupled training while their weights diverge, and give provable CKA/RSA lower bounds. Empirically, NSCL tracks CL more than SCL or CE, and alignment grows with class count and temperature and depends on the batch-size/learning-rate scaling. They concede the bounds are loose and vacuous beyond the first few epochs at scale. They claim confirmation 'across datasets and architectures', but only ResNet-50 is used.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares SimCLR-style decoupled contrastive learning with NSCL, SCL and cross-entropy using ResNet-50 models; it does not reproduce either cited original source's method. The theory analyzes coupled CL/NSCL runs with shared initialization and randomness.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment varies with class count, temperature, batch size and learning-rate scaling; it also tends to decrease as training progresses. The text reports CKA and RSA trends in the class-count and temperature experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Supervised models (SCL, CE) reach equal or higher linear-probe accuracy than CL, yet CL–SCL CKA is only 0.043 on the same data and architecture.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Comparably capable models trained on the same data with different objectives need not have aligned representations.

fits_no_version.finding: Alignment depends on batch size via learning-rate scaling: it decreases with B under O(B) scaling and increases under the other three scalings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Measured cross-objective alignment depends on optimization hyperparameters.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code and a project page are available but supplies no URL in the text
record.problems: The reported empirical comparisons use a ResNet-50 setup rather than a model-size or capability sweep. CL and supervised models share vision datasets and architecture; the theoretical coupling assumes shared initialization, batches and augmentations and uses a similarity-descent surrogate. The paper notes that its theoretical bounds can become vacuous beyond the first few epochs of large-scale training. Most alignment curves are figures without tabulated values, and no uncertainty estimates for alignment are stated.
record.rows_left_out: Individual curve values and detailed objective-by-objective trajectories across every dataset and epoch in Figures 2–5 and 7 are not separately extracted because the text does not tabulate them; the explicit cross-dataset trends and the stated Tiny-ImageNet example are recorded above. Downstream accuracy results in Table 1 and weight-gap plots in Figure 6 are omitted because they do not measure the claim's representational alignment versions.

untested.parts: No model-size or capability sweep. Only ResNet-50 is used; no independently trained models with different architectures or data are compared.
No vision–language or paired image–caption alignment.
No comparison of independently initialized seeds of the same objective. The theory assumes shared initialization.
No linear mapping, stitching, relative representations or unpaired alignment.
No neuron, SAE-feature or circuit universality.
No designed comparison of similarity measures, neighbour settings or OOD inputs. CKA and RSA on the same cosine matrix, and train vs test sets, merely agree.
Does not separate shared data from a common model of reality across modalities or architectures. Plateau with scale is not tested.

missing.what: CL–CE alignment trajectory, which dips early and then rises, and its values relative to SCL
Fig. 1 CIFAR-100 result: CKA/RSA stay high while the weight gap grows; representation-space angle 27.8° vs weight-space 85.7°

record.verdict_notes: V6 'challenges' in the record is dropped. Temperature, class count and batch size are training conditions, not measurement choices, and CKA and RSA on the same cosine matrix are not a meaningful metric contrast. The text does not say whether the empirical runs share initialization and batches as the theory assumes; if they do, the pairs are not independently trained, which weakens relevance to V1/V7. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size or capability sweep; no independently trained models spanning different architectures, data or modalities are compared for alignment as scale increases.
No paired image-caption or other vision-language representations are compared.
The coupled theoretical runs share initialization and randomness; the study does not compare independently initialized seeds or test shared features/subspaces across seeds.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation or unpaired alignment method is tested.
No recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features or circuits are measured.

Compares CKA and RSA and reports some train/test-set results. Does not vary nearest-neighbour settings or systematically test alternative similarity settings, out-of-distribution inputs, or whether alignment vanishes under such choices.

Tests CL against NSCL, SCL and cross-entropy in the reported vision setups, and studies some training-condition dependencies. Does not isolate shared data or objectives from a common model of reality as competing causal explanations; does not establish a general plateau or quantify incompleteness across diverse architectures and modalities.

rows.subject: Coupled CL and NSCL similarity-descent recursions
rows.operation_detail: Proves a high-probability upper bound on the Frobenius distance between CL and NSCL similarity matrices over training.
rows.value: Theorem 1 bounds the distance by exp((1/(2τ²B)) Σηt) · (1/(τ√B)) Σηt ΔC,δ(B;τ), with probability at least 1 − δ.
rows.uncertainty: High-probability guarantee; probability at least 1 − δ
rows.note: The result is conditional on the stated coupled surrogate and shared randomness; it is a bound, not an empirical distance measurement.
rows.check: A theoretical bound on coupled similarity-descent surrogates with shared randomness, not a measurement of alignment. The authors say it becomes vacuous beyond the first few epochs.
